messages.subject: accounting for topography; plant distance sampling
messages.subject_clean: accounting for topography; plant distance sampling
messages.body_plain:
My colleagues and I have recently used line transect distance sampling to=
 estimate density of flowering stems of a tall, very brightly-flowered fo=
rb in grassland.  The plant is visible with the naked eye up to 150 m awa=
y. However, hills often obstruct our view (For instance, a small ridge wi=
th its crest 15 m east of the observer will restrict detection distance t=
o 15 m in that direction, whereas we may be able to view these plants 150=
 m to the west). I would like suggestions on how to best analyze data fro=
m these surveys.

 I have used MCDS to account for variation in detectability due to habita=
t; for instance, using grassland vegetation height as a covariate, with f=
ocal organisms in areas with taller grasses being slightly more difficult=
 to see than in areas with shorter grasses.  But in our current study, as=
 we walk a transect, the existence of small hills to one side or the othe=
r make detection beyond the hill impossible (unless we create and walk mo=
re transects, which is an option). But even if we create more transects, =
how should we analyze the distance data from each transect, when maximum =
detection distance can change so greatly along the transect due to hills?=

If you like, please email responses to me:

mor...@iastate.edu

I would be happy to compile the responses I receive and summarize them to=
 the list.

-Ray Moranz

Beginning immediately following the Conference on Biology of Marine
Mammals (3 December), The University of St. Andrews is happy to announce
that we will be delivering an Introduction to Distance Sampling workshop
in Tampa Florida.  We have not presented a workshop in North America
since 2009, and we haven't delivered a workshop in eastern North America
since 2005.  If you happen to be attending the Marine Mammal Conference,
you can attend this workshop immediately thereafter.

The workshop will last four days (3-6 Dec.) and will cover introductory
topics in distance sampling.  Instructors will include Prof. Steve
Buckland and Dr. Len Thomas, as well as several other lecturers and
demonstrators from the University of St. Andrews.

We are in the process of finalising the arrangements with the hotel
where we will conduct the workshop, so we are not yet accepting
registration for the workshop.  However, we expect this workshop to fill
quickly (limit of 35 participants), so our early registration deadline
is 31 August.  We expect official registration to open before the end of
July; but get in contact with us at the web address below ahead of that
with questions and expressions of interest.

Please visit the workshop website to learn more details as well as send
an expression of interest visit:

http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance.workshops/floridaoverview.html

Hello all,

I'm doing line transect distance sampling in North Madagascar in order=20

to estimates nocturnal lemurs densities.

But their are 2 species of lemurs that we never (or rarely) see on=20
transect but that we can hear really easily, because they sing mainly at=20

the moment we are doing night survey (Phaner and Eulemur).

And in all the forest it is obvious for us that they occur at high=20
densities.

In order to complete our study I'm planning to do Point count distance=20
sampling survey using animal vocals and estimating distance to observer.=20
But point count is new to me and none of the member of the team have=20
experience in it.

I'm wondering if this kind of survey would limit our analysis capacity=20
to encounter frequencies or relative densities....as we are violating=20
one of the assumption of the method : the distance from the observer=20

cannot be measured acurately.

If you have answers to my problem, suggestion to resolve it, ....

I think people doing bird survey can be confronted to the same problem=20
but quickly going true the litterature (available to me in madagascar=20
now) I have not been able to find answers to my question, clear and=20

simples protocols to do Point count distance sampling...

If you have good protocole, nice bibliograpics items, and nice answers,=20

you'd make my life aesier.
...

Thanks all of you

messages.body_plain:
Dear Jordi,

If your problem is using the acoustic data to apply conventional=20
distance sampling, that is in fact what happens for many bird surveys in=20
closed canopy habitats, and essentially people usually assume that=20
measurement error is small.

However, some published work implies that might not be the case, e.g.

Alldredge, M. W.; T. R. Simons & Pollock, K. H. A field evaluation of=20
distance measurement error in auditory avian point count surveys Journal=20
of Wildlife Management, 2007, 71, 2759-2766

On the other hand, if you need references on acoustic density surveys=20
you could use both

(using SECR for birds)

Dawson, D. K. & Efford, M. G. Bird population density estimated from=20
acoustic signals Journal of Applied Ecology, 2009, 46, 1201-1209

or

(using CDS for whales)

Marques, T. A.; Munger, L.; Thomas, L.; Wiggins, S. & Hildebrand, J. A.=20
Estimating North Pacific right whale (Eubalaena japonica) density using=20
passive acoustic cue counting Endangered Species Research, 2011, 13, 163-=
172

How you will see from this last reference, you have a potential problem=20
in relating the density of sounds to the density of animals, but this=20
can be solved in 2 ways: (1) using a cue rate (as we did in the above=20
reference) or assuming you can uniquely identify each bird to an animal=20
(as I believe Dawson and Efford have).

As an aside, I would be interested in knowing more details about your=20
study, as we are finalizing a review paper on estimating animal density=20
from acoustics data and yours seems like an interesting setting.

I hope this helps,

Cheers

Tiago

Jessie:

You don't mention in your message what was unsuccessful about your first
analysis, so it is a bit hard to suggest a remedy.  However ...

Seems you would be best advised to perhaps consider the days to be
strata, and you might wish to make inference about the average number of
dogs over the sampling events.  The days might then be considered as a
sample of possible days on which you could conduct your surveys.  Have a
look through Chapter 8 of the Distance Users Guide wherein a discussion
of strata as replicates can be found.

Brendan, the usual problem with large aggregations of seaduck (aside from e=
stimating the number of birds in a cluster) is that you cannot sensibly ide=
ntify a single location for a cluster.  Even if you can, then the effective=
 width of search for the really large aggregations is an order of magnitude=
 larger than for small groups.  You can in principle stratify by cluster si=
ze - e.g. 3 strata, of small, medium and large clusters, possibly with the =
3rd stratum being treated as a strip transect (complete count within the su=
rveyed strip).  But number of detected clusters is then typically very smal=
l, perhaps just one, for the large cluster stratum.  Also, such large clust=
ers can extend across more than one transect line.

Using aerial visual surveys, the best strategy is perhaps to collect distan=
ce data in intervals, e.g. placing markers on the wing struts, with aligned=
 markers on the windows, to ensure the observers count birds in the right i=
nterval.  You then just count numbers of birds detected in each distance in=
terval, without attempting to record clusters at all.

In the UK, we have switched to using high resolution video or stills, which=
 allows a complete count of birds to be done within the strip (which tends =
to be narrower than for visual surveys).  The data are then analysed using =
strip transect methods.  Again, this avoids the need to define clusters.  W=
e also fit spatial density surfaces, e.g. to assess impact of windfarm deve=
lopments.

Steve Buckland

Maja, that is not really the same issue, as you don't have such a problem o=
f cluster definition.  Also, in the seabird case, interest is in how many i=
ndividuals there are, not in how many clusters/flocks there are, whereas in=
 your case, you're interested in the number of clusters/territories.

I see no reason why point transect methods would not work for territories. =
 You can estimate territory location from e.g. the midpoint of detections t=
hat are deemed to relate to a single territory.  If that location is very c=
lose to the point, it seems highly likely that the territory will be identi=
fied even if the bird is not detected at every visit, so certain detection =
at the point seems a reasonable assumption.  Variability in detectability d=
epending on where the bird is located inside its territory should not be a =
problem.  If territories were very large, then you might need more visits t=
o ensure certain identification of a territory that is centred at the point=
.

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

We are considering using distance sampling to estimate the density of 19
species of nonnative invasive plants along roads and trails within national
parks.  The area of inference would be roads and trails (and a buffer
around them) because this is considered a high-risk area for weeds.  A
different sampling approach will be applied to interior parklands.

Our concern is that the density of invasive plants along trails is
inversely related to distance from the trail, i.e., that objects are not
distributed in the area to be sampled according to some stochastic process,
and we'd like to be able to locate our sampling transects or point on the
trail.  Given that a GRTS draw would be used to locate transects or points
along trails, is it absolutely necessary to randomly orient transects
and/or locate points in the buffered trail area?  In many cases, thick
vegetation and steep topography make going off trail impractical.  If we
are to use distance sampling, it would have to be from the road/trail.
Buckland et al. (2009) stated "more general methods of Buckland et al. (in
prep) allow estimation in these circumstances.....  Fortunately, the bias
from this source is negligible for the large majority of studies."

Is there methodology that you can point us to in the Advanced Distance
Sampling book (it's in the mail)? Other suggestions?

Thanks for any assistance you can provide!

Stacey Ostermann-Kelm
NPS Inventory & Monitoring Program
